question: What problem does real-time collaborative editing solve, and what does 'convergence' mean?
answer_hinglish:
Collaborative editing ka core problem hai: kai log ek hi document ko EK SAATH edit kar rahe hain, aur har user apna change turant apni screen pe dekhna chahta hai -- network round trip ka wait kiye bina. Toh har client ke paas document ki apni local copy hoti hai, aur concurrent edits alag-alag order mein alag copies pe lagte hain.

Simple example (yeh `LEARNING_GUIDE.md` mein bhi hai): doc mein "ac" hai. Alice position 1 pe "X" daalti hai, Bob usi waqt position 1 pe "Y". Agar dono ke changes ko as-is doosre ki copy pe apply kar do, toh Alice ke paas "aXYc" aur Bob ke paas "aYXc" -- documents diverge ho gaye. Ya worse: agar Bob ne pehle kuch delete kiya tha, toh Alice ka "position 5" ab galat jagah point karega.

Convergence ka matlab: jab sab edits sab jagah pahunch jayein (system quiet ho jaye), toh har client ka document aur server ka document EXACTLY same hona chahiye. Saath mein intention preservation bhi chahiye -- Alice ka "X" wahin aaye jahan usne socha tha.

Mere project mein yeh Operational Transformation (OT) se solve hota hai: server har op ko ek revision number deta hai, aur concurrent ops ko `transform()` se adjust karta hai. Tests jaise `test_two_users_edit_concurrently_and_converge` aur fuzz test exactly yahi assert karte hain: `a.doc == b.doc == server content`.
why_needed: Yeh poore project ka 'kyun' hai. Agar convergence clearly define nahi kar sakte toh OT, sequencer, ordered forwarder -- kuch bhi justify nahi hoga.
real_world_analogy: Do log ek hi shopping list ki apni-apni photocopy pe likh rahe hain. Shaam ko dono lists merge karni hain aur dono ke paas exactly same list honi chahiye -- bina kisi ka item khoye.
how_it_works: Har client optimistic local apply karta hai, op server ko bhejta hai. Server ops ko total order deta hai aur transform karke store karta hai. Clients baaki ops receive karke apne pending ops ke against transform karke apply karte hain. End mein sab same text pe pahunchte hain.
in_this_project: `LEARNING_GUIDE.md` Step 1 mein exact 'ac' example hai. `tests/test_ot.py::test_concurrent_insert_same_position_tie_break` mein `apply(apply(doc, a), bp) == apply(apply(doc, b), ap) == 'aXYc'` assert hota hai. End-to-end: `tests/test_realtime.py::test_two_users_edit_concurrently_and_converge` final content `'Alice: , world!!!'` check karta hai.
code_example:
# real, from tests/test_ot.py
doc = "ac"
a, b = TextOp([1, "X", 1]), TextOp([1, "Y", 1])
ap, bp = transform(a, b)
assert apply(apply(doc, a), bp) == apply(apply(doc, b), ap) == "aXYc"
advantages: Har user zero-latency local typing dekhta hai
Final state deterministic aur sabke liye same
disadvantages: Correctness subtle hai -- naive merging fail hota hai
Server ko ordering aur transform dono sambhalne padte hain
common_mistakes: Convergence ko 'last write wins' samajhna -- usme edits khote hain
Sirf convergence check karna, intention preservation bhool jana
follow_up_questions: Convergence aur intention preservation mein kya farak hai?
Locking (ek time pe ek editor) se yeh problem kyun nahi solve karte?
Tumhare tests convergence kaise prove karte hain?

question: Why did you use WebSockets instead of HTTP polling or Server-Sent Events?
answer_hinglish:
Short answer: collaborative editing mein traffic dono directions mein chhote messages ka hai -- har keystroke-batch client se server jata hai aur doosron ke ops server se client aate hain -- aur latency tens of milliseconds mein chahiye. WebSocket ek full-duplex TCP connection deta hai jo open rehta hai, toh na har message pe HTTP request overhead, na polling delay.

HTTP polling (har 1s pe "kuch naya hai?") ke do problems: latency polling interval jitni ho jati hai, aur jab kuch naya nahi hai tab bhi requests ka load. Long polling better hai par har message ke baad naya request, headers, aur ordering sambhalna mushkil.

SSE (Server-Sent Events) server -> client push ke liye achha hai, simple hai, HTTP pe chalta hai, auto-reconnect bhi hai. Lekin woh one-way hai: client ke ops ke liye phir bhi alag HTTP POST chahiye. Toh ek op ka ack (SSE pe) aur op submit (POST pe) do alag channels pe honge, aur ordering reasoning complex ho jati hai. Mere design mein ack bhi ordered stream se aata hai, toh ek single bidirectional channel cleaner hai.

Costs bhi honest bataunga (`SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` mein likhe hain): WebSocket stateful hai -- load balancer ko upgrade headers aur long timeouts chahiye, har connection memory leta hai, reconnect logic aur application-level heartbeat (`ping`/`pong`) khud likhna padta hai. Mere project mein `/ws` endpoint `collab/api.py` mein hai, aur editor har 10s pe `ping` bhejta hai.
why_needed: Interviewer pehle transport choice pe hi probe karta hai; trade-off clear bolna senior signal hai.
real_world_analogy: Polling = har 5 minute pe dost ko call karke poochna 'kuch hua?'. SSE = radio -- sirf sun sakte ho. WebSocket = phone call jo chalu rehti hai, dono bol sakte hain.
how_it_works: Client HTTP GET bhejta hai `Upgrade: websocket` header ke saath; server 101 Switching Protocols deta hai; uske baad wahi TCP connection pe frames dono taraf jaate hain jab tak koi close na kare.
in_this_project: `collab/api.py::ws_endpoint` JSON messages handle karta hai: client -> `join`, `op`, `cursor`, `ping`; server -> `joined`, `op`, `ack`, `presence`, `cursor`, `error`, `pong` (`API_DOCUMENTATION.md`). `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` ka section 'Why WebSockets (not HTTP polling)' yahi reasoning deta hai. `editor.html` mein `setInterval(()=>send({type:'ping'}),10000)` heartbeat hai.
advantages: Low latency, bidirectional
Per-message overhead bahut kam
Ek channel pe op, ack, presence sab ordered
disadvantages: Stateful connections -- LB/timeouts/reconnect ki complexity
Memory per connection
Heartbeats khud implement karne padte hain
common_mistakes: SSE ko 'kamzor WebSocket' samajhna -- one-way push ke liye SSE often better hai
Reconnect aur catch-up design kiye bina WebSocket use karna
follow_up_questions: Agar sirf server->client notifications hote toh kya choose karte?
WebSocket connections ko load balancer ke peeche kaise chalate ho?
HTTP/2 ya WebTransport ka kya role ho sakta hai?

question: How is a WebSocket connection established, and what does a reverse proxy like nginx need to support it?
answer_hinglish:
WebSocket ek normal HTTP/1.1 request se shuru hota hai. Client `GET /ws?ticket=...` bhejta hai headers `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: Upgrade`, `Sec-WebSocket-Key` ke saath. Server agar agree kare toh `101 Switching Protocols` aur `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` return karta hai. Uske baad wahi TCP connection HTTP nahi rehta -- us pe WebSocket frames (text/binary/ping/pong/close) dono directions mein chalte hain.

Problem yeh hai ki `Upgrade` aur `Connection` hop-by-hop headers hain -- reverse proxy by default unhe forward nahi karta. Isliye nginx ko explicitly batana padta hai. Mere `deploy/nginx.conf` mein teen cheezein hain:

1. `proxy_http_version 1.1` -- upgrade HTTP/1.0 mein nahi hota.
2. `proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;` aur `proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;` -- `map` block se `Connection` header 'upgrade' ya 'close' set hota hai.
3. `proxy_read_timeout 3600s` -- nginx default 60s mein idle connection kaat deta hai; editor khula hai par koi type nahi kar raha toh socket mar jayega. Client ka 10s `ping` bhi isme madad karta hai.

Ek aur point: upstream plain round-robin hai -- `upstream collab { server collab1:8000; server collab2:8000; }` -- koi sticky session nahi, kyunki koi bhi server koi bhi document serve kar sakta hai (sequencing Postgres mein, fan-out Redis se).

Close codes bhi handshake ke baad application level pe use hote hain: 4401 bad ticket, 4403 no access, 4400 malformed, 1013 client too slow.
why_needed: Production mein WebSocket ka sabse common outage proxy config hota hai -- 60s pe connections drop hona ya upgrade fail hona.
real_world_analogy: Jaise kisi office ki reception pe normal visitor ki tarah aao (HTTP), aur phir guard tumhe private meeting room ki chaabi de de (101 upgrade) -- ab wahan bina reception ke baat chalti hai.
how_it_works: HTTP handshake -> 101 -> framed protocol over same TCP. Proxy ko hop-by-hop headers forward karne hote hain aur long-lived connection ke liye idle timeouts badhane hote hain.
in_this_project: `deploy/nginx.conf`: `map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade { default upgrade; '' close; }`, `proxy_read_timeout 3600s; # idle WebSockets would otherwise be cut after 60s`. `DEPLOYMENT.md` bhi kehta hai: 'Load balancer: WebSocket upgrade headers + long proxy_read_timeout. Sticky sessions NOT required.'
advantages: Ek hi port pe HTTP aur WS dono
Round-robin kaafi hai, sticky routing nahi chahiye
disadvantages: Proxy/LB har layer pe sahi configure karna padta hai (CDN, ALB, nginx)
Long timeouts ke saath dead connections detect karne ke liye heartbeats chahiye
common_mistakes: `proxy_http_version 1.1` bhool jana
Default 60s read timeout chhod dena aur phir 'random disconnects' debug karna
Hop-by-hop headers ko automatically forwarded maan lena
follow_up_questions: Agar LB connection kaat de toh client kya karta hai?
L4 vs L7 load balancer WebSockets ke liye?
Graceful deploy mein open sockets ka kya hota hai?

question: Explain Operational Transformation in simple terms.
answer_hinglish:
Operational Transformation (OT) ek technique hai jisme hum document ki state ko nahi, balki EDITS (operations) ko bhejte hain, aur jab do edits concurrently (ek doosre ko dekhe bina) bane hon, toh ek edit ko doosre ke hisaab se "transform" (adjust) kar dete hain taaki dono orders mein apply karne pe same result aaye.

Example: doc "abc". Alice ne position 0 pe "X" daala -> "Xabc". Bob ne usi waqt position 2 wala "c" delete kiya (Bob ke liye "ab"). Ab Bob ka delete Alice ke document pe lagana hai. Alice ke doc mein "X" aage aa gaya, toh "c" ab position 3 pe hai, 2 pe nahi. Transform yahi karta hai: Bob ke delete ko Alice ke insert ke against shift karke "position 3 delete" bana deta hai. Dono end mein "Xab" pe pahunchte hain.

Formal property TP1 hai: `apply(apply(S, a), b') == apply(apply(S, b), a')` jahan `(a', b') = transform(a, b)`.

Mere project mein OT `collab/ot.py` mein hai, ot.js / Google Wave ke TextOperation model jaisa: op ek list hai -- positive int = retain, string = insert, negative int = delete -- jo poore document ko left se right cover karta hai. Ek central server (Postgres row lock) sab ops ko total order deta hai, isliye sirf TP1 chahiye. Clients optimistic apply karte hain aur server ke ops ko apne pending ops ke against transform karte hain.

Google Docs aur Etherpad historically OT based hain -- `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` table mein yeh likha hai.
why_needed: OT is project ka dil hai; har aage ka sawaal (TP1, compose, sequencer) isi pe based hai.
real_world_analogy: Do log ek hi kitaab ke page numbers ke reference de rahe hain. Agar ek ne beech mein naya page jod diya, toh doosre ka 'page 50' ab 'page 51' ho gaya -- transform yeh reference update karna hai.
how_it_works: Ops positions ke relative hote hain. transform dono ops ko saath mein walk karta hai: doosre ka insert aaye toh hum utna retain badhate hain; dono delete karein toh duplicate delete hata dete hain.
in_this_project: `collab/ot.py` docstring: 'Operational Transformation for plain text (the ot.js / Google-Wave TextOperation model)'. Functions: `apply`, `compose`, `transform`, `transform_index`, `diff_op`. Server side `service.submit` aur client side `client.py::_server_op` dono `transform` use karte hain.
code_example:
# illustrative using this repo's API
from collab.ot import TextOp, transform, apply
doc = "abc"
alice = TextOp([ "X", 3])        # insert X at 0
bob   = TextOp([2, -1])          # delete 'c'
ap, bp = transform(alice, bob)
assert apply(apply(doc, alice), bp) == apply(apply(doc, bob), ap) == "Xab"
advantages: Ops chhote hote hain (state nahi bhejte)
Server authority: validate, authorize, persist karna aasan
disadvantages: Transform functions sahi likhna mushkil
Central ordering chahiye (P2P mein TP2 problem)
common_mistakes: OT ko 'diff and merge' (git style) samajhna -- OT real-time, fine-grained, deterministic hota hai
Transform ko sirf index shifting samajhna -- delete overlap aur ties bhi handle karne hote hain
follow_up_questions: TP1 kya hai?
OT aur CRDT mein kya farak hai?
Tie kaise break karte ho jab dono same jagah insert karein?

question: What is a revision number, and why does every operation the client sends carry a base_rev?
answer_hinglish:
Revision number document ki version counter hai. `documents.rev` 0 se shuru hota hai aur har committed op usko 1 badhata hai -- rev 1, 2, 3... `operations` table mein har row ka `rev` woh revision hai jo us op ne PRODUCE ki. Toh rev N ka op document@rev(N-1) pe apply hota hai aur document@revN deta hai.

`base_rev` client ka statement hai: "Maine yeh op document ki revision X dekh ke banaya." Yeh zaroori hai kyunki jab op server pe pahunchta hai, tab tak doosre users ke ops commit ho chuke ho sakte hain. Server ko pata hona chahiye ki kaun se ops client ne NAHI dekhe -- woh exactly `rev > base_rev` wale ops hain. `service.submit` unhi ko load karke incoming op ko ek-ek karke transform karta hai.

Example (`ARCHITECTURE.md` sequence): client A ne base_rev 7 pe op bheja; server pe head 9 hai. Server op ko rev 8 ke against transform karta hai, phir rev 9 ke against, phir apply karke rev 10 store karta hai.

Validation bhi hota hai: `if base_rev < 0 or base_rev > doc.rev: raise InvalidOperation(...)` -- client future revision claim nahi kar sakta.

Client side `CollabClient.rev` "last server revision we have applied" hai; `_send_op` usi ko `base_rev` bhejta hai. Ack aur incoming ops dono `self.rev` update karte hain.
why_needed: Base revision ke bina server ko pata hi nahi chalega ki op ko kis context se transform karna hai -- OT ka poora contract isi pe khada hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise kisi shared Google Sheet pe comment: 'Version 7 dekh ke maine row 5 change ki'. Reviewer ko pata hai version 8 aur 9 mein kya badla, toh woh tumhara 'row 5' adjust kar sakta hai.
how_it_works: Server: lock doc row -> history = ops WHERE rev > base_rev ORDER BY rev -> op = transform(op, h)[0] for each -> apply -> rev = head + 1.
in_this_project: `collab/service.py::submit`: `history = SELECT op FROM operations WHERE document_id = :d AND rev > :b ORDER BY rev`. Migration comment: `rev bigint NOT NULL, -- the revision this op PRODUCED (1, 2, 3 ...)` aur `op jsonb NOT NULL, -- already transformed: applies to the doc at rev - 1`. `client.py::_send_op` mein `"base_rev": self.rev`.
code_example:
# real, collab/service.py (trimmed)
if base_rev < 0 or base_rev > doc.rev:
    raise InvalidOperation(f"base revision {base_rev} is not in [0, {doc.rev}]")
history = (await s.execute(text("SELECT op FROM operations WHERE document_id = :d AND rev > :b ORDER BY rev"),
                           {"d": doc_id, "b": base_rev})).scalars().all()
for h in history:
    op = transform(op, TextOp.from_json(h))[0]
advantages: Server exactly jaanta hai kis cheez ke against transform karna hai
Catch-up (last_rev) aur history same counter use karte hain
disadvantages: Bahut purana base_rev = lambi history ke against transform (cost)
common_mistakes: Client ka base_rev bhejne ke bajaye server ka current rev assume karna
Revision ko timestamp se replace karna -- clocks total order nahi dete
follow_up_questions: Client bahut purane base_rev ke saath aaye toh?
Rev counter gaps ho sakte hain kya?
Ack aane pe client ka rev kaise update hota hai?

question: What is a 'room' in your WebSocket server, and how do rooms relate to documents and servers?
answer_hinglish:
Room ek in-memory grouping hai: "is server pe, is document ke liye kaun-kaun se connections khule hain". `realtime.py` mein `Room` dataclass mein `doc_id`, `conns: dict[conn_id, Conn]`, `next_rev`, `buffer`, `lock` aur `gap_task` hain. `Hub.rooms` ek dict hai `doc_id -> Room`.

Important point: room PER SERVER hota hai, global nahi. Agar Alice server 1 pe hai aur Bob server 2 pe, dono same document edit kar rahe hain, toh server 1 pe bhi ek Room hai (sirf Alice ke saath) aur server 2 pe bhi ek Room (sirf Bob ke saath). Dono servers ko ek doosre ke ops Redis pub/sub channel `collab:doc:{id}` se milte hain, aur har server apne local room ke connections ko forward karta hai.

Room lifecycle: pehla connection `Hub.join` mein `self.rooms.setdefault(doc_id, Room(doc_id))` se room banata hai aur `room.next_rev = head + 1` set karta hai (ordered stream wahan se shuru). Aakhri connection `Hub.leave` mein room ko dict se hata deta hai aur `gap_task` cancel karta hai.

Room ke andar ka `next_rev` aur `buffer` "ordered forwarder" ka state hai -- yeh guarantee karta hai ki is server ke saare connections ko ops strictly revision order mein milein. `/stats` endpoint `rooms: {doc_id: number_of_conns}` dikhata hai, toh ops team dekh sakti hai kis server pe kaunse documents active hain.
why_needed: Room concept samjhe bina multi-server fan-out aur ordered delivery samajh nahi aayega.
real_world_analogy: Ek company ke har city office mein ek project ka meeting room hai. Mumbai room mein Mumbai wale, Delhi room mein Delhi wale; dono rooms ek conference line (Redis) se jude hain.
how_it_works: join: room get-or-create under room.lock, register conn. Pub/sub message -> rooms.get(doc_id) -> ordered forwarder -> har conn ki queue. leave: conn hatao; khaali ho toh room drop.
in_this_project: `collab/realtime.py`: `class Room` (fields `conns`, `next_rev`, `buffer`, `lock`, `gap_task`), `Hub.join`, `Hub.leave`, `Hub._on_message` (`room = self.rooms.get(m.get('doc_id')); if room is None: return` -- jis doc ka local room nahi, uska message ignore). `/stats` `api.py` mein.
code_example:
# real, collab/realtime.py
@dataclass
class Room:
    doc_id: str
    conns: dict[str, Conn] = field(default_factory=dict)
    next_rev: int = 1
    buffer: dict[int, dict] = field(default_factory=dict)
    lock: asyncio.Lock = field(default_factory=asyncio.Lock)
    gap_task: asyncio.Task | None = None
advantages: Local fan-out cheap hai (in-memory)
Room state per server isolated -- koi cross-server lock nahi
disadvantages: Har server ko har doc ke messages milte hain (psubscribe *), chahe room ho ya nahi
Room state crash pe kho jata hai (lekin reconstructable hai Postgres se)
common_mistakes: Room ko global maan lena
Room ko lock ke bina create/delete karna -- join/leave race (real bug tha)
follow_up_questions: Room delete aur naya join ek saath ho toh kya hota hai?
Ek server pe 10k rooms ho toh memory?
Room ka next_rev kahan se initialize hota hai?

question: Why are presence and cursors stored in Redis and not in Postgres?
answer_hinglish:
Presence ("kaun abhi document mein hai") aur cursors ("Bob ka cursor position 42 pe hai") EPHEMERAL data hain: bahut frequently change hote hain, kuch seconds mein purane ho jate hain, aur agar kho jayein toh koi nuksaan nahi -- next ping ya cursor move unhe wapas bana dega. Aisa data durable relational DB mein likhna galat fit hai: har cursor move pe Postgres write = WAL, row versions, vacuum pressure, aur sequencer ke row lock wale DB pe extra load.

Redis in-memory hai, fast hai, aur sab servers share karte hain -- toh server 2 pe baitha user bhi server 1 wale users ko dekh sakta hai. Mere project mein presence ek Redis hash hai `collab:presence:{doc_id}`: field = `conn_id`, value = JSON `{user_id, name, client_id, ts, cursor, server}`. `Hub.join` `hset` karta hai, `Hub.leave` `hdel`, aur `Hub.touch` (har `ping` aur `cursor` message pe) `ts` refresh karta hai.

Staleness: agar server crash ho jaye toh `leave` kabhi nahi chalega aur hash entry pada rahega. Isliye `Hub.presence()` read time pe filter karta hai: `if now - d['ts'] <= presence_stale_seconds` (default 30s). Crashed server ke users 30s mein list se gayab.

Cursors live broadcast bhi Redis pub/sub se hote hain (`type: cursor`), lekin unhe ordered forwarder se NAHI guzarna padta -- `_on_message` unhe seedha room ke doosre conns ko bhej deta hai. Ordering/loss yahan acceptable hai.

Golden rule: document content aur ops = Postgres (source of truth); presence/cursors/tickets = Redis (ephemeral).
why_needed: Data ko uski durability requirement ke hisaab se store karna system design ka basic sense hai.
real_world_analogy: Office ka attendance register (Postgres) vs reception pe 'abhi kaun andar hai' whiteboard (Redis). Whiteboard mitt bhi jaye toh koi baat nahi.
how_it_works: hset on join, hdel on leave, touch on ping/cursor updates ts, presence() filters by ts age. Cursor messages pub/sub pe unordered broadcast.
in_this_project: `collab/realtime.py`: `Hub.presence` (stale filter), `Hub.touch`, `Hub.join` (`hset f'collab:presence:{doc_id}'`). Config `presence_stale_seconds: int = 30`. Test `test_presence_and_cursors` do servers pe check karta hai ki alice ko bob ka join event mile aur `/docs/{id}/presence` dono names de.
code_example:
# real, collab/realtime.py
async def presence(self, doc_id: str) -> list[dict]:
    raw = await self.redis.hgetall(f"collab:presence:{doc_id}")
    now, out = time.time(), []
    for cid, v in raw.items():
        d = json.loads(v)
        if now - d["ts"] <= self.cfg.presence_stale_seconds:   # entries of crashed servers age out
            out.append({"conn_id": cid.decode() if isinstance(cid, bytes) else cid, **d})
    return out
advantages: Cheap high-frequency writes
Cross-server visibility
Postgres sequencer pe load nahi
disadvantages: Redis restart pe presence khatam (agle ping tak)
Stale entries hash mein padi rehti hain (sirf read pe filter)
common_mistakes: Cursor positions ko DB mein persist karna
Staleness timeout na rakhna -- crashed server ke 'ghost users' hamesha dikhenge
follow_up_questions: Stale entries hash se kabhi delete hoti hain?
Per-field TTL kaise karoge?
Cursor position concurrent ops ke baad galat ho jaye toh?

question: How is a text operation represented in your OT library (retain/insert/delete, base_length, target_length)?
answer_hinglish:
Op ek list of components hai jo document ko LEFT SE RIGHT walk karti hai:
- positive int `n` = retain: n characters skip karo (as-is rakho)
- string `s` = insert: yeh text yahan daalo
- negative int `-n` = delete: agle n characters hata do

Important rule: op POORE document ko cover karta hai. Isliye har op ke do lengths hain: `base_length` = jis document pe apply hota hai uski length (retain + delete ka sum), aur `target_length` = apply ke baad ki length (retain + insert ka sum).

Example: "hello" -> "hello world" ka op `[5, " world"]` hai: base 5, target 11. "abc" -> "XaYc": `["X", 1, -1, "Y", 1]`: 'X' insert, 'a' retain, 'b' delete, 'Y' insert, 'c' retain.

Whole-document coverage ka fayda validation hai: `apply()` sabse pehle `len(doc) != op.base_length` check karta hai aur OTError raise karta hai. Toh agar client ka op galat revision ke against bana hai, ya malicious hai, toh woh silently galat jagah apply nahi hoga -- reject ho jayega. `test_apply_basic` mein `apply("abc", TextOp([2, "x"]))` OTError deta hai kyunki op sirf 2 chars cover karta hai.

Wire format bhi yahi JSON list hai (`to_json` / `from_json`), aur Postgres mein `jsonb` column mein store hota hai. Yeh ot.js ka TextOperation model hai, isliye JS port (`editor.html`) bhi 1:1 same hai.
why_needed: Har aage ka algorithm (apply/compose/transform) isi representation pe chalta hai; isko crisp explain karna zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek tape recorder ka edit script: 'pehle 5 second chalao, phir yeh naya clip jodo, phir 2 second kaat do, phir baaki chalao'. Script poori tape cover karti hai.
how_it_works: Builder methods `retain/insert/delete` lengths update karte hain; `apply` doc pe pointer `i` chalata hai -- retain copy karta hai, insert append, delete pointer aage badhata hai bina copy ke.
in_this_project: `collab/ot.py::TextOp` (`__slots__ = ('ops', 'base_length', 'target_length')`), `is_retain/is_insert/is_delete`, `apply`. `tests/test_ot.py::test_apply_basic` covers `[5, ' world']`, `[5, -6]`, `['X', 1, -1, 'Y', 1]`.
advantages: Compact JSON wire format
Length check se galat-context ops pakde jaate hain
Same model JS aur Python mein
disadvantages: Har op ka size document position pe depend (badi retain numbers), lekin components count chhota
Plain text only -- formatting attributes nahi
common_mistakes: Op ko (position, text) tuple samajhna -- multi-span edits express nahi honge
base_length check skip karna
follow_up_questions: Ek op mein multiple inserts/deletes ho sakte hain?
Position-based op ke bajaye yeh format kyun?
Unicode / surrogate pairs ka length JS vs Python mein farak?

question: What is normalisation in TextOp, and why is 'insert before delete' the canonical form?
answer_hinglish:
Normalisation ka matlab: ek hi edit ke multiple representations ko ek canonical form mein laana, taaki ops compare ho sakein aur algorithms simple rahein. TextOp ke builders khud normalise karte hain:

1. Adjacent same-type components merge hote hain: `retain(2).retain(3)` -> `[5]`, `insert('a').insert('b')` -> `['ab']`, `delete(1).delete(2)` -> `[-3]`.
2. Zero-length components drop hote hain (`retain(0)`, `insert('')` no-op).
3. Insert aur delete same position pe hon toh insert PEHLE aata hai: `TextOp().delete(2).insert('x')` -> `['x', -2]`.

Point 3 kyun? "pehle 2 chars delete karo phir x daalo" aur "pehle x daalo phir 2 chars delete karo" same result dete hain. Agar dono forms allowed hon toh `__eq__` (jo `self.ops == other.ops` compare karta hai) do equal ops ko unequal bolega, aur compose/transform ke branches mein extra cases aayenge. ot.js bhi yahi convention use karta hai.

Implementation `insert()` mein hai: agar last component delete hai, toh agar uske pehle insert hai usme append karo, warna delete ko ek step aage shift karke uski jagah insert rakh do.

Interesting twist: yahi normalisation ek real finding ki wajah bani. `compose(s1, s2)` mein s2 ka insert s1 ke delete ke aage move ho jata hai, jisse concurrent insert ke saath tie-break flip ho sakta hai -- isliye transform compose pe distribute nahi karta (`test_transform_does_not_distribute_over_compose`). Toh canonical form ka side effect design pe asar dalta hai.
why_needed: Normalisation equality, testing aur compose/transform ki correctness ka base hai -- aur yahan ek subtle design consequence bhi hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise fractions ko lowest terms mein likhna: 2/4 aur 1/2 same hain, par compare karne ke liye sab ko 1/2 bana dete ho.
how_it_works: retain/delete last component same type ho toh add; insert: last insert ho toh concat, last delete ho toh insert ko delete ke pehle rakho.
in_this_project: `collab/ot.py::TextOp.insert` (comment: 'Canonical form: insert before delete'). Test `test_normalisation_merges_components`: `[5, 'ab', -3]` aur `['x', -2]`.
advantages: Ops ka structural equality meaningful
Algorithms mein kam cases
Wire size chhota
disadvantages: Canonical form insert ki relative position delete ke saath badal deta hai -- tie-break semantics pe asar
common_mistakes: Constructor ko bypass karke raw list ops banana (non-normalised)
Socha ki normalisation pure cosmetic hai
follow_up_questions: Normalisation se tie-break kaise flip hua?
from_json bhi normalise karta hai kya?
Equality ke liye semantic compare kyun nahi?

question: What exactly does transform(a, b) return and guarantee? Walk through an example.
answer_hinglish:
`transform(a, b)` do ops leta hai jo SAME document pe concurrently bane (dono ka base_length same), aur `(a', b')` return karta hai jahan:
- `a'` = a ko b ke baad apply karne layak version
- `b'` = b ko a ke baad apply karne layak version
- Guarantee (TP1): `apply(apply(S, a), b') == apply(apply(S, b), a')`

Yani "a phir b'" aur "b phir a'" dono same document dete hain -- diamond close ho jata hai.

Example `test_concurrent_delete_overlap`: doc "abcdef". a = `[1, -3, 2]` (delete "bcd"), b = `[2, -3, 1]` (delete "cde"). Overlap "cd" hai. transform: pehle 1 char dono retain -> dono mein retain 1. Phir a ka 'b' delete vs b ka retain -> a' mein delete 1. Phir 'cd' dono delete -> kisi ko dobara delete nahi karna, dono skip. Phir 'e': a retain, b delete -> b' mein delete 1. Last 'f' retain. Result: a' = `[1, -1, 1]` (b ke baad 'e' delete), b' = `[1, -1, 1]` -- dono paths "af" dete hain.

Doosra example `test_delete_vs_insert_inside_deleted_range`: a ne "bcde" delete kiya, b ne 'c' aur 'd' ke beech "XYZ" insert kiya. Result "aXYZf" -- insert survive karta hai, kyunki insert hamesha pehle handle hota hai aur deleted range uske around split ho jati hai.

Server pe hum sirf `transform(op, h)[0]` use karte hain (incoming op ka transformed version); client pe dono outputs chahiye -- pending op ko bhi update karna hai aur server op ko bhi.
why_needed: TP1 hi convergence ka mathematical contract hai; yeh clearly bol pana core interview signal hai.
real_world_analogy: Do log ek hi map pe route draw kar rahe hain. Transform kehta hai: 'agar tum dusre ka route pehle follow karo, toh tumhara route aise adjust hoga' -- dono ka destination same aayega.
how_it_works: Dono ops ko saath mein walk karo. Insert kisi ka bhi ho -> output mein insert, doosre mein retain. Retain/retain -> dono retain min. Delete/delete -> dono skip. Delete/retain -> sirf deleter ke output mein delete.
in_this_project: `collab/ot.py::transform` docstring: 'a and b were made concurrently on the same document. Returns (a', b') so both paths converge.' Randomized check `test_property_transform_converges` (5 seeds x 400 = 2000 cases).
code_example:
# real, tests/test_ot.py
def test_concurrent_delete_overlap():
    doc = "abcdef"
    a, b = TextOp([1, -3, 2]), TextOp([2, -3, 1])     # delete "bcd" vs delete "cde"
    ap, bp = transform(a, b)
    assert apply(apply(doc, a), bp) == apply(apply(doc, b), ap) == "af"
advantages: Simple diamond property, property-test karna easy
O(len(a)+len(b)) linear walk
disadvantages: Sirf two-op property hai; multi-party ke liye ordering discipline chahiye
common_mistakes: transform(a,b) aur transform(b,a) ko symmetric maan lena -- tie-break asymmetric hai
Overlapping deletes ko dono outputs mein rakhna (double delete)
follow_up_questions: Insert inside a deleted range survive kyun karta hai?
Kya transform commutative hai?
Property test kaise likha?

question: How does your OT break ties when two users insert at the same position?
answer_hinglish:
Tie tab hota hai jab dono ops exact same position pe insert karte hain. Kisi ek ko left jaana padega -- aur yeh decision DETERMINISTIC hona chahiye, warna server aur clients alag order choose karenge aur diverge ho jayenge.

Mere `transform(a, b)` mein rule simple hai: `a`'s inserts win, yani left jaate hain. Code mein `if is_insert(o1)` check `if is_insert(o2)` se PEHLE hai -- toh jab dono ke current component insert hain, a ka insert output mein pehle jaata hai aur b' mein uske liye retain aata hai.

`test_concurrent_insert_same_position_tie_break`: doc "ac", a = X at 1, b = Y at 1 -> dono paths "aXYc".

Ab sawaal: real system mein 'a' kaun hai? Server pe `op = transform(op, h)[0]` -- incoming op `a` hai aur already-committed history op `b` hai. Matlab LATE arriving op ka insert committed op ke LEFT jata hai. Client pe `_server_op` mein `transform(outstanding, server_op)` -- client ka pending op `a` hai. Dono jagah consistent hai: "pending/incoming op = a, committed op = b". Isi consistency ki wajah se client aur server same text pe pahunchte hain. Agar server ek convention use kare aur client ulta, toh tie pe divergence hoga.

Yeh "fair" nahi hai (kaun pehle commit hua usse farak nahi padta), lekin fairness requirement nahi hai -- determinism aur consistency hai. Kuch systems site_id ya user_id se tie-break karte hain, khaaskar P2P mein jahan 'committed' ka concept nahi hota.
why_needed: Ties sabse common divergence bug hain; interviewer zaroor poochta hai 'same position pe dono type karein toh?'.
real_world_analogy: Do log ek saath darwaze pe pahunche. Rule hai 'jo andar aane ki request kar raha hai woh pehle' -- rule kuch bhi ho, bas sab guards ek hi rule follow karein.
how_it_works: Branch order decide karta hai: o1 insert ho toh pehle emit, warna o2 insert. Server aur client dono 'pending op as first argument' convention follow karte hain.
in_this_project: `collab/ot.py::transform`: `if is_insert(o1):  # tie-break: a's inserts win (go left)`. Server: `service.submit` mein `transform(op, TextOp.from_json(h))[0]`. Client: `client.py::_server_op` mein `transform(out, op)` aur `transform(self.buffer, op)`.
code_example:
# real, collab/ot.py
if is_insert(o1):                       # tie-break: a's inserts win (go left)
    ap.insert(o1)
    bp.retain(len(o1))
    o1 = next(i1)
    continue
if is_insert(o2):
    ap.retain(len(o2))
    bp.insert(o2)
    o2 = next(i2)
    continue
advantages: Deterministic, koi metadata nahi chahiye
Central server ke saath consistent argument order kaafi hai
disadvantages: Order 'fair' nahi (arrival order se relate nahi)
Argument order galti se ulta hua toh silent divergence
common_mistakes: Client aur server mein transform arguments ka order alag rakhna
Tie-break ke liye timestamps use karna (clocks skewed)
follow_up_questions: P2P mein tie-break kaise karte?
Agar client transform(server_op, pending) call kare toh kya tootega?
Kya user ko order matter karta hai?

question: What is the difference between TP1 and TP2, and why does your design only need TP1?
answer_hinglish:
TP1 (Transformation Property 1): do concurrent ops a, b ke liye `S . a . b' == S . b . a'`. Do-op diamond close hona chahiye. Yeh mera `transform` satisfy karta hai, aur `test_property_transform_converges` 2000 random cases pe check karta hai.

TP2: teen concurrent ops ke liye -- op c ko "a phir b'" ke against transform karna aur "b phir a'" ke against transform karna SAME result dena chahiye: `T(T(c, a), b') == T(T(c, b), a')`. Yani transform ka result path-independent hona chahiye. Yeh tab chahiye jab koi central order nahi -- P2P system mein alag peers ops ko alag orders mein receive karte hain aur har peer apne order mein transform karta hai.

TP2 notoriously hard hai: famous OT papers (dOPT, adOPTed, SOCT) ke transform functions TP2 counterexamples ke saath fail hue the -- insert/delete ties ke edge cases ('false-tie' puzzle). Practically har production OT system TP2 avoid karta hai.

Mera design TP2 avoid karta hai central sequencer se: Postgres row lock har op ko unique revision deta hai -- total order. Server incoming op ko history ke against EXACT revision order mein transform karta hai, aur har client bhi ops ko usi revision order mein receive karta hai (ordered forwarder) aur apne pending ops ko unhi ke against ek-ek karke transform karta hai. Har jagah transformation path same hai, toh path-independence ki zarurat nahi -- sirf TP1 chahiye. `ot.py` docstring yahi bolta hai: 'Peer-to-peer OT without a central order also needs TP2, which is notoriously hard -- that's where CRDTs are usually preferred.'

Yeh Jupiter / Google Wave approach hai: client-server, har client sirf server ke saath 2-party OT karta hai.
why_needed: Yeh distinguish karna batata hai ki tumhe OT ki theory pata hai aur tumne architecture choice consciously ki.
real_world_analogy: TP1: do raaste ek hi mod tak pahunchte hain. TP2: teesra traveller kisi bhi raaste se aaye, uska final location same hona chahiye. Agar sabko ek hi fixed route pe chalao (central server), toh TP2 ki chinta hi nahi.
how_it_works: Central sequencer -> single history line. Har party (server, har client) transform ka same sequence follow karti hai. TP1 + same sequence => convergence.
in_this_project: `collab/ot.py` module docstring, `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` 'Convergence argument' (4 steps), `service.submit` one-by-one loop, `realtime.py::_deliver_ordered`.
advantages: TP1 simple aur testable
Central order se proven-hard problem avoid
disadvantages: Server mandatory -- P2P/offline-first nahi
Sequencer single point of ordering per doc
common_mistakes: Sochna ki TP1 test pass = multi-party convergence guaranteed (ordering discipline bhi chahiye)
Clients ke beech direct op exchange add karna (TP2 territory)
follow_up_questions: TP2 counterexample ka example de sakte ho?
CRDT TP2 problem kaise avoid karte hain?
Agar ordering ek jagah break ho jaye toh kya hoga?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: TP1-only design simple aur provable hai, lekin har edit ke liye server ka total order zaroori hai -- offline/P2P support limited.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar kisi bug se do servers same doc ke ops alag order mein forward karein (e.g. ordered forwarder skip ho), toh clients alag sequences pe transform karenge aur TP2 jaisi divergence aayegi.
advanced.alternatives: TP2-satisfying OT (complex, historically buggy), ya CRDTs (Yjs, Automerge) jo commutativity data structure se guarantee karte hain.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Per-document total order 10x/100x pe bhi same rehta hai; scaling documents ke across horizontal hota hai, ek doc ke andar nahi. Hot doc ke liye in-memory sequencer.
advanced.production_improvements: Convergence ko production mein verify karne ke liye periodic checksum: client apne doc ka hash rev ke saath bheje, server compare kare aur mismatch pe force-resync.

question: What does compose(a, b) do, and where does your system use it?
answer_hinglish:
`compose(a, b)` do SEQUENTIAL ops (b, a ke baad wale document pe bana) ko ek single op mein jod deta hai jo same effect deta hai: `apply(doc, compose(a, b)) == apply(apply(doc, a), b)`. Precondition: `a.target_length == b.base_length`, warna OTError.

Kahan use hota hai? Client ke buffer mein. Jab client ka ek op in-flight hai (outstanding, ack ka wait), user typing jaari rakhta hai. Har naya keystroke op turant local doc pe apply hota hai aur buffer mein compose hota hai: `self.buffer = op if self.buffer is None else compose(self.buffer, op)`. Jab ack aata hai, poora buffer EK op ban ke jata hai. Iska matlab 50 keystrokes ek round trip ke dauraan = 1 op, 50 nahi. Yeh natural batching hai aur isi wajah se per-document throughput limit (45-66 ops/s) human editing ke liye kaafi hai.

Offline mein bhi yahi: saare offline edits buffer mein compose hote rehte hain, reconnect pe ek op jata hai.

Correctness: `test_property_compose_equals_sequential_apply` 2000 random cases pe check karta hai.

Ek important caveat jo maine property test se seekha: transform compose pe distribute NAHI karta -- `transform(c, compose(s1, s2))` hamesha `transform(transform(c, s1)[0], s2)[0]` ke barabar nahi hota (tie-break flip). Isliye server history ke ops ko compose karke ek baar transform nahi karta; ek-ek karke karta hai. Client side buffer compose karna safe hai kyunki buffer ek hi author ke sequential ops hain aur server unhe ek op ki tarah treat karta hai.
why_needed: compose batching ka mechanism hai aur ek important correctness subtlety ka source bhi.
real_world_analogy: Do instructions 'seedha 5 km jao' aur 'phir 2 km aur jao' ko ek instruction 'seedha 7 km jao' bana dena.
how_it_works: Dono ops ko saath walk: a ka delete seedha output (b ne woh text dekha hi nahi), b ka insert seedha output; a ka insert + b ka delete = cancel; a ka insert + b ka retain = insert; retain+delete = delete; retain+retain = retain.
in_this_project: `collab/ot.py::compose`; `collab/client.py::edit` (`compose(self.buffer, op)`); `editor.html` input handler `buf=buf?compose(buf,op):op`. Test `test_property_compose_equals_sequential_apply`.
code_example:
# real, collab/client.py
async def edit(self, op: TextOp) -> None:
    self.doc = apply(self.doc, op)
    self.buffer = op if self.buffer is None else compose(self.buffer, op)
    await self._flush_buffer()
advantages: Natural keystroke batching -> kam ops, kam DB writes
Offline edits ek op mein
disadvantages: Composed op mein individual edit granularity history mein nahi dikhti
Bada buffer = bada op (max_op_components limit)
common_mistakes: compose aur transform ko interchangeable samajhna
History ko compose karke ek baar transform karna (non-distributive)
follow_up_questions: compose ka insert-then-delete case kaise cancel hota hai?
Buffer kitna bada ho sakta hai?
Undo ke liye compose kaafi hai?

question: How does transform handle overlapping deletes and an insert inside a concurrently deleted range?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh do edge cases hain jahan naive OT implementations galti karte hain.

1) Overlapping deletes: dono users ne kuch common text delete kiya. Agar dono transformed ops mein woh delete rahe, toh doosra apply karte waqt woh text pehle hi gayab hai -- double delete, galat characters udd jayenge ya length mismatch. Mera transform `delete/delete` branch mein `m = min(-o1, -o2)` chars ke liye KISI output mein kuch nahi likhta -- "both deleted the same text: nobody needs to delete it again". Bas dono iterators aage badhte hain. Non-overlapping parts `delete/retain` aur `retain/delete` branches mein jate hain, jahan sirf deleter ke transformed op mein delete aata hai.

`test_concurrent_delete_overlap`: "abcdef", a deletes "bcd", b deletes "cde" -> dono "af".

2) Insert inside deleted range: Alice ne "bcde" delete kiya, Bob ne 'c' aur 'd' ke beech "XYZ" daala. Do choices: Bob ka text bhi delete kar do, ya survive karne do. Mera transform insert ko HAMESHA pehle process karta hai (insert ki koi base length nahi hoti), toh Bob ka insert transformed op mein aata hai aur Alice ka delete uske around do hisson mein split ho jata hai. Result "aXYZf" -- `test_delete_vs_insert_inside_deleted_range`.

Kyun survive? Intention preservation: Bob ne jaan boojh ke naya text likha jo Alice ne kabhi dekha hi nahi; usko delete karna Bob ka kaam silently khona hoga. Google Docs bhi aisa hi behave karta hai.
why_needed: Interviewers edge cases se depth check karte hain; yeh do classic cases hain.
real_world_analogy: Do safai karne wale ek hi kamra saaf kar rahe hain -- jo cheez ek ne pehle hi phek di, doosra usse dobara phekne nahi jayega. Aur agar kisi ne beech mein naya gamla rakh diya, toh woh nahi phekna.
how_it_works: delete/delete: consume min from both, emit nothing. delete/retain: ap.delete. retain/delete: bp.delete. Insert branches first, so inserts never get swallowed by deletes.
in_this_project: `collab/ot.py::transform` branch `elif is_delete(o1) and is_delete(o2):` ; tests `test_concurrent_delete_overlap`, `test_delete_vs_insert_inside_deleted_range`.
code_example:
# real, collab/ot.py
elif is_delete(o1) and is_delete(o2):   # both deleted the same text: nobody needs to delete it again
    m = min(-o1, -o2)
    o1, o2 = (o1 + m) or next(i1), (o2 + m) or next(i2)
elif is_delete(o1) and is_retain(o2):
    m = min(-o1, o2)
    ap.delete(m)
    o1, o2 = (o1 + m) or next(i1), (o2 - m) or next(i2)
advantages: No double delete
Concurrent inserts kabhi silently lost nahi
disadvantages: Kuch users expect kar sakte hain ki deleted section mein typed text bhi chala jaye
common_mistakes: Delete overlap ko dono transformed ops mein rakhna
Insert ko deleted range ke saath delete kar dena
follow_up_questions: Agar dono ne exactly same range delete kiya toh transformed ops kya honge?
Rich text mein formatting overlap kaise handle hota?
Undo ke saath overlap delete ka kya hoga?

question: Explain the counterexample showing that transform does not distribute over compose, and why it forces the server to transform against history one revision at a time.
answer_hinglish:
Pehle property: kya `transform(c, compose(s1, s2))` == `transform(transform(c, s1)[0], s2)[0]` hai? Agar hota, toh server history ke saare ops compose karke EK transform kar sakta tha -- faster. Maine yeh property test likha aur woh FAIL hua; shrinking ke baad minimal counterexample mila jo ab `test_transform_does_not_distribute_over_compose` mein hai.

Setup: doc = "heoo". s1 = `[3, -1]` (last 'o' delete), s2 = `[3, "2"]` (end pe "2" insert). Concurrent client op c = `["aYYbZ", -3, 1, "221"]` (start pe "aYYbZ", 3 chars delete, 1 retain, end pe "221").

compose(s1, s2) normalise hota hai `[3, "2", -1]` -- insert-before-delete canonical form. Matlab s2 ka "2" ab deleted 'o' ke PEHLE baith gaya, jabki sequential mein woh delete ke BAAD tha. Client ka "221" insert bhi end pe hai -- 'o' ke baad. Stepwise path mein, s1 ke baad 'o' gayab, phir c ka "221" aur s2 ka "2" same position pe tie karte hain -> c pehle -> "...2212". Composed path mein s2 ka "2" delete se pehle hai, toh ab c ka insert aur "2" alag positions pe hain; tie ka nature badal gaya -> "...2221". Stepwise "aYYbZ2212" vs composed "aYYbZ2221".

Dono individually 'converge' karte hain, par ALAG answers pe. Agar server composed path le aur client stepwise (kyunki client ops ek-ek karke receive karta hai), toh divergence.

Design consequence: sabko SAME sequence of transforms follow karni hai. `service.submit` history ka har op ek-ek karke apply karta hai -- `for h in history: op = transform(op, TextOp.from_json(h))[0]` -- exactly jaise client `_server_op` mein har rev pe karta hai.
why_needed: Yeh project ki sabse strong 'maine test se seekha' story hai -- property testing ki value aur ek subtle correctness insight dono dikhati hai.
real_world_analogy: Do baar 1 km chalne aur ek baar 2 km chalne ka distance same hai -- par agar beech mein ek traffic signal hai jahan 'pehle kaun' decide hota hai, toh ek saath nikalne pe signal pe order alag ho sakta hai.
how_it_works: compose normalisation insert ko delete ke aage shift karta hai; isse insert ki 'position relative to concurrent insert' change hoti hai; tie-break rule (a left) ab different pair pe apply hota hai.
in_this_project: `tests/test_ot.py::test_transform_does_not_distribute_over_compose` (docstring explains). `service.py` header: 'transform the incoming op against them ONE BY ONE (same sequence the client sees; transform does not distribute over compose -- see tests/test_ot.py)'. `FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md` bug #3 'False property'.
code_example:
# real, tests/test_ot.py
doc = "heoo"
client = TextOp(["aYYbZ", -3, 1, "221"])
s1, s2 = TextOp([3, -1]), TextOp([3, "2"])
stepwise = apply(apply(apply(doc, s1), s2), transform(transform(client, s1)[0], s2)[0])
composed_s = compose(s1, s2)
assert composed_s.ops == [3, "2", -1]                       # insert moved before the delete
composed = apply(apply(doc, composed_s), transform(client, composed_s)[0])
assert stepwise == "aYYbZ2212" and composed == "aYYbZ2221" and stepwise != composed
advantages: Finding ko test ke roop mein freeze kiya -- regression nahi hoga
Design rule clear: same sequence everywhere
disadvantages: Server history ka har op alag se transform karta hai -- long catch-up mein O(history) transforms
common_mistakes: Optimisation ke naam pe history compose karke ek transform karna
Property test fail hone pe property ko sach maan ke code 'fix' karna -- yahan property hi galat thi
follow_up_questions: Property test ne minimal case kaise diya (shrinking)?
Client side buffer compose karna phir safe kyun hai?
Kya different tie-break rule se distributivity aa jati?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: One-by-one transform correctness deta hai aur client ke sequence se match karta hai; cost: bahut purane base_rev pe N transforms per submit, row lock ke andar.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi future optimisation history compose kare, toh rare ties pe silent divergence -- sirf fuzz/property tests pakdenge, production mein 'kabhi kabhi doc alag' type bug.
advanced.alternatives: Tie-break ko position+site-id based banana jo normalisation se independent ho; ya CRDT jahan har char ki stable identity hoti hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x stale clients (offline) ke saath history transforms lock time badhayenge; base_rev ki max staleness limit lagao (bahut purana ho toh force resync), ya transform lock ke bahar karo optimistic retry ke saath.
advanced.production_improvements: Property tests CI mein zyada seeds ke saath, aur ek long-running fuzz nightly; client-side checksum se divergence detection.

question: Describe the client OT state machine: Synchronized, AwaitingConfirm, AwaitingWithBuffer.
answer_hinglish:
Client ek waqt pe server pe sirf EK unacknowledged op rakhta hai. Isse state machine banti hai (ot.js wala model, `client.py` aur `editor.html` dono mein):

1. Synchronized: koi pending op nahi (`outstanding is None and buffer is None`, yaani `settled`). User edit kare -> op local apply, turant bhejo -> AwaitingConfirm.
2. AwaitingConfirm: ek op (`outstanding = (client_seq, op)`) bheja hai, ack ka wait. Naya edit -> local apply, `buffer` mein rakho -> AwaitingWithBuffer.
3. AwaitingWithBuffer: outstanding + buffer. Aur edits -> `compose(buffer, op)`.

Events:
- Ack aaya: `outstanding = None`, `rev = ack.rev`. Buffer hai toh woh naya outstanding banke naye `client_seq` ke saath jata hai (AwaitingConfirm), warna Synchronized.
- Server op S aaya (kisi aur ka): `outstanding', S' = transform(outstanding, S)`; `buffer', S'' = transform(buffer, S')`; `S''` local doc pe apply; `rev = S.rev`. Pending edits doosron ke edits ke UPAR baithe rehte hain.

Ek waqt pe ek op kyun? Kyunki outstanding op ka base_rev fixed hai; agar do ops in-flight hon toh doosre ka base_rev pehle ke ack pe depend karega -- complexity. Ek op in flight + composed buffer = simple, aur natural batching.

Mera extension: ot.js mein 'buffer without outstanding' state nahi hai, par mere offline mode mein hai (`ARCHITECTURE.md` mein `OfflineBuffer` state). Isi state ne fuzz test mein bug diya -- agla sawaal.
why_needed: Server design tabhi samajh aata hai jab client ka contract clear ho; ack ordering aur dedupe isi state machine ke liye bane hain.
real_world_analogy: Courier counter pe ek hi parcel ek time pe bhejte ho; jab tak receipt (ack) nahi aati, naye items ek bade box (buffer) mein pack karte rehte ho, receipt aate hi box bhej dete ho.

# real, collab/client.py
async def _flush_buffer(self) -> None:
    if self.outstanding is None and self.buffer is not None and self.connected and self.joined.is_set():
        seq, op = self.next_seq, self.buffer
        self.next_seq += 1
        self.buffer = None
        self.outstanding = (seq, op)
        await self._send_op(seq, op)

question: Walk through the end-to-end convergence argument for your system.
answer_hinglish:
Main isko 4 steps mein bolta hoon (`SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` 'Convergence argument'):

1. Total order: `service.submit` document row pe `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` leta hai. Ek document ke liye ek waqt pe ek hi transaction op commit kar sakta hai, chahe kitne bhi servers hon. Har op ko unique `rev = head + 1` milta hai. `operations (document_id, rev)` primary key us order ko persist karta hai.

2. Server transform: incoming op `base_rev` pe bana tha; server sirf `rev > base_rev` wale ops ke against, EK-EK karke, revision order mein transform karta hai. Stored op already transformed hai -- doc@rev-1 pe directly apply hota hai.

3. Client delivery order: har client ko ops strictly revision order mein milte hain -- ordered forwarder (`_deliver_ordered`) out-of-order pub/sub messages ko buffer karta hai aur gaps Postgres se fill karta hai. Apne op ka ack bhi isi stream se, sahi position pe aata hai. Client apne outstanding aur buffer ko har incoming op ke against, isi order mein, ek-ek karke transform karta hai.

4. TP1: har step pe client aur server ek hi pair (pending, committed) ka diamond close kar rahe hain, aur TP1 (property-tested) guarantee karta hai ki dono sides same text dekhte hain. Kyunki sequence same hai, aur transform compose pe distribute nahi karta, "same sequence" yahan load-bearing hai.

Result: jab system quiet hota hai, har client ka `doc` == server ka `documents.content`. Fuzz test (6 clients, 2 servers, 25 random edits each, 2 offline/reconnect, 2 seeds) exactly yeh assert karta hai -- `all(c.doc == final['content'])` aur `all(c.rev == final['rev'])`.
why_needed: Senior interview mein 'tumhe kaise pata yeh converge karta hai?' sabse important sawaal hai -- argument + evidence dono chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek orchestra: conductor (sequencer) beat deta hai, har musician (client) usi beat pe apna part adjust karta hai; sab same sheet music follow karte hain toh gaana ek jaisa sunai deta hai.
how_it_works: Total order + same transform sequence on both sides + TP1 => equal state at quiescence.

disadvantages: Teen components (sequencer, forwarder, client) mein se kisi ek ka ordering bug poora argument tod deta hai

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Argument ek strict ordering chain pe depend karta hai (DB -> Redis -> forwarder -> client); simplicity vs har link ko reliable banane ki cost.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Redis message loss -> gap fill; tail loss (last op lost, aur koi naya op nahi) -> review mein yeh gap mila tha (client next op/reconnect tak stale); ab `Hub.check_tails` har `tail_check_ms` (1s) DB head se compare karke missing revs deliver karta hai, toh staleness ~1s tak bounded hai.
advanced.alternatives: CRDT-based convergence (order-independent), ya durable ordered log (Kafka/Redis Streams) jisme gap detection offsets se automatic ho.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Zyada clients se argument nahi badalta; per-doc total order hi bottleneck rehta hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Client periodic `(rev, hash(doc))` report kare; server mismatch pe full resync bheje; metrics mein divergence count.

question: What does transform_index do, and how are cursor positions kept correct during concurrent edits?
answer_hinglish:
`transform_index(op, index)` batata hai ki ek cursor position `index` op apply hone ke baad kahan chali jaayegi. Rules: cursor ke PEHLE insert -> cursor right shift (insert length jitna); cursor ke pehle delete -> cursor left shift; delete range cursor ko cover kare -> cursor delete start pe aa jata hai.

Implementation: `index` ko remaining distance ki tarah use karta hai aur `new_index` result. Retain pe `index -= c`; insert pe `new_index += len(c)`; delete pe `new_index -= min(index, -c)` aur `index += c`. Jaise hi `index < 0` (cursor ke aage nikal gaye), loop break -- uske baad ke components cursor ko affect nahi karte.

Test `test_transform_index_cursor`: `[2, "XYZ", 3]` ke liye cursor 1 -> 1, cursor 4 -> 7. `[1, -3, 2]` (chars 1..3 delete) ke liye 0 -> 0, 2 -> 1, 5 -> 2.

Edge: cursor exactly insert position pe ho, toh retain ke baad `index` 0 hota hai (not < 0), loop chalta hai aur insert cursor ko right push karta hai. Matlab doosre ka insert tumhare cursor ke LEFT aata hai -- tumhara cursor text ke baad.

Is project mein kahan use? Honestly bataunga: browser `editor.html` mein `tIndex` apne hi textarea ke selection ko server op ke baad adjust karta hai (`setText(next, op)`), taaki remote edit aane pe tumhara caret jump na kare. Remote users ke cursors server pe transform NAHI hote -- `README.md` limitation: 'Cursor positions are transformed client-side; the server stores the last reported position only.' Cursor message mein `rev` bhejte hain taaki receiving client usse transform kar sake.
why_needed: Cursors ke bina collaborative editor unusable lagta hai; aur yeh OT ka doosra practical use hai.
real_world_analogy: Kitaab mein bookmark: agar kisi ne pichle chapters mein pages jode, toh bookmark ka page number badh jaata hai, lekin woh same jagah pe rehta hai.
how_it_works: Op ko left se walk karo, remaining distance track karo; inserts before cursor add, deletes before cursor subtract (capped by cursor position).
in_this_project: `collab/ot.py::transform_index`, `editor.html` `tIndex` + `setText(next, op)`, cursor messages `api.py` mein `{position, selection_end, rev}`. `README.md` known limitations.
advantages: O(components) cheap
Local caret stable rehta hai
disadvantages: Remote cursors server-side transform nahi hote -- stale rev pe position thoda galat dikh sakta hai
common_mistakes: Cursor ko absolute position maan ke as-is broadcast karna
Cursor exactly insert point pe ho toh left/right convention bhool jana

question: Why does the client keep only one operation in flight and compose the rest into a buffer?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki ek in-flight op ke saath protocol simple aur correct rehta hai. Har op ke saath `base_rev` jata hai -- "maine yeh doc@rev X pe banaya". Agar client ek op bheje (base 7) aur ack se pehle doosra op bheje, toh doosra op pehle op ke BAAD wale doc pe bana hai -- uska base pehle op ka resulting rev hai, jo client ko abhi pata hi nahi (server ne usse 8 diya ya 12, depends on concurrency). Server ko phir 'client ke apne unacked ops' ka chain track karna padta. ot.js model is complexity ko ek simple rule se hata deta hai: ek outstanding, baaki buffer.

Buffer ka matlab: ack aane tak ke saare local edits `compose()` se ek op mein jud jaate hain. Ack aate hi `_flush_buffer` buffer ko naye `client_seq` aur latest `self.rev` (ack ka rev) ke base ke saath bhejta hai. Ab base_rev bilkul clear hai.

Side benefit -- automatic batching: agar round trip 20ms hai aur user tez type kar raha hai, toh 20ms ke saare keystrokes ek op ban jate hain. Slow network pe aur bade batches, toh server pe op rate naturally limited. `TESTING.md` isi ko point karta hai: 'real users rarely exceed a few ops/s each because clients compose keystrokes while an op is in flight'. Isliye per-document 45-66 ops/s limit humans ke liye kaafi hai.

Cost: high-latency link pe doosre users ko tumhare edits bade chunks mein dikhte hain, thoda 'jumpy'.
why_needed: Yeh design decision throughput, simplicity aur correctness teeno ko jodta hai.
real_world_analogy: Lift ek hi time pe ek trip karti hai; jab tak woh upar gayi hai, neeche log jama hote rehte hain aur agli trip mein sab ek saath jaate hain.
how_it_works: outstanding set hai toh naya edit buffer mein compose; ack pe buffer -> outstanding -> send with base_rev = ack rev.

question: What is diff_op and where is it used?
answer_hinglish:
`diff_op(old, new)` do strings leta hai aur ek TextOp banata hai jo `old` ko `new` mein badal de. Algorithm simple 'common prefix + common suffix' hai, real diff (Myers/LCS) nahi:

1. Shuru se kitne characters same hain -> prefix length `p`.
2. Aakhir se (prefix ke baad ke hisse mein) kitne same hain -> suffix `s`.
3. Op = `retain(p)`, `delete(len(old) - p - s)`, `insert(new[p:len(new)-s])`, `retain(s)`.

Toh beech ka badla hua hissa ek block mein replace hota hai. Builders normalise karte hain, toh zero-length parts drop ho jaate hain aur canonical form insert-before-delete banta hai.

Kahan use hota hai:
1. Restore: `service.restore_op(current, old)` = `diff_op(current, old)`. Version restore ek NAYA op hai jo current text ko purane text mein badalta hai -- sequencer se normally guzarta hai, live editors ko dikhta hai.
2. Browser editor: `editor.html` mein textarea `input` event pe `diffOp(doc, now)` -- textarea ka purana value vs naya value. Ek keystroke ya paste ka diff hamesha ek contiguous change hai, toh prefix/suffix kaafi hai.

Limitation: agar do door-door ke changes ek saath hon (e.g. restore jahan purane version mein shuru aur aakhir dono alag the), toh beech ka sab kuch delete+reinsert ho jata hai. Concurrent edits jo us beech wale hisse mein the, unke liye yeh 'replace' semantics hai. Minimal diff (Myers) restore ko gentler bana sakta tha. `test_diff_op` correctness (`apply(old, diff_op(old,new)) == new`) check karta hai.
why_needed: Restore aur browser input dono isi pe chalte hain; iski limitations batana honesty dikhata hai.
real_world_analogy: Do photos compare karke sirf beech ka badla hua hissa kaat ke naya chipka dena -- edges same rakho.
how_it_works: Prefix scan, suffix scan (bounded by min length - p), phir retain/delete/insert/retain builder.
